l5-bankroll: Why Is Bankroll Management So Important?
Even if you're a world-class player, without adequate bankroll management, one unlucky downswing can bankrupt you. Bankroll management is the safety net that protects you from variance.
Golden rule: at least 20-30 buy-ins for cash games, 50-100 buy-ins for tournaments.

Cash games (NLH):
- Minimum: 20 buy-ins
- Recommended: 30-50 buy-ins
- Pro standard: 50+ buy-ins

Example: playing $1/$2 (buy-in $200), you need at least $4,000-$10,000 dedicated.
Never mix living expenses with your poker bankroll! Keeping them separate is the first principle of bankroll management.

Move up: accumulate 30 buy-ins of the next stake in your current game
Move down: decisively move down when your bankroll drops below 20 buy-ins of the current stake

Moving down isn't shameful! Many world-class players moved down during downswings, then climbed back.
Bankroll management is one of the biggest differences between pros and recreational players. Without bankroll discipline, even great technique is just gambling.

Kelly Criterion formula:
f* = (bp - q) / b

Where f* = optimal bankroll fraction
b = net odds (win b times the bet)
p = win probability
q = loss probability = 1-p

Poker application:
Assume you have a 60% win-rate edge at 1:1 odds
f* = (1×0.6 - 0.4) / 1 = 0.2 = 20%
That is, never bet more than 20% of your total bankroll

Conservative (Half Kelly): f = f*/2 = 10%, further reducing ruin risk

Theory reference: the quantitative application of the Kelly Criterion to poker bankroll management is in Theory Academy T8 “Bankroll Management Psychology”, which fully covers bankroll methodology in poker psychology.

Counter-intuitive: the optimal betting fraction under the Kelly Criterion is far lower than intuition suggests. Even with a 60% win-rate edge, Kelly only recommends committing 20% of your bankroll. Most players actually commit far more than Kelly's recommended value — one of the main causes of ruin.
l5-tilt: Tilt is a state where negative events (bad beats, losing streaks, opponent taunts, etc.) cause emotional swings that lead to irrational decisions. Tilt is the poker player's biggest enemy — it costs far more than skill gaps.
The cost of tilt often exceeds the cost of skill gaps. A $10/hr winner can lose $500+ in one serious tilt session.

1. Anger tilt: furious raising/bluffing after a bad beat
2. Fear tilt: afraid to bet or over-folding after losses
3. Revenge tilt: irrational actions targeting one specific opponent
4. Desperation tilt: playing too many hands to win back losses fast

1. Stop-loss: set a maximum session loss (e.g. 2 buy-ins) and stop when reached
2. Rest rule: take a 5-10 minute break every hour
3. Self-awareness: regularly check your emotional state
4. Long-term perspective: remind yourself this is one hand, not your whole life
5. Stop signal: stop immediately when you notice yourself taking "out-of-character" actions

Pros don't never tilt — they recognize it faster and take action. Learning to "stop-loss" is the most important emotional-management step. Remember: there's always another session tomorrow, but once the money's gone it's gone.

Tendler's 7 Tilt profiles quick reference:
1. Anger tilt — emotional loss of control after bad beats
2. Frustration tilt — negative emotions from a long downswing
3. Fear tilt — overcautious decisions from fear of losing
4. Self-destructive tilt — subconsciously punishing yourself
5. Boredom tilt — attention dropping during long sessions
6. Ego tilt — overconfidence after a winning streak
7. Urgency tilt — rushed decisions from time or money pressure

Recognition signals: pause training when you miss 3 questions in a row or accuracy drops >15%

Theory reference: the complete analysis of Tendler's 7 tilt profiles is in Theory Academy T8 Chapter 1 "Tilt Recognition and Classification", including recognition signals, triggers, and responses for each profile.

Counter-intuitive: when accuracy drops, stopping matters more than continuing. Many players choose "one more hand to win it back" during emotional swings, but this is the most dangerous mistake — decision quality drops significantly while tilting, so continuing only expands the loss.
l5-game-selection:
Good game selection can double your hourly win rate. Look for tables with:
- A high share of recreational players (VPIP > 30%)
- Larger average pots
- Higher flop rate (many players seeing the flop)
- More interaction between players (frequent raises)
Whether you're the 6th-best or 1st-best player at the table matters more than which stake you play.

Poker is a long-term game. Short-term results (1 day, 1 week, even 1 month) are heavily luck-influenced. Only at a large enough sample (10,000+ hands) does the skill gap show.

Don't move up stakes because of short-term luck beyond your bankroll, and don't abandon correct strategies because of short-term bad luck.

The pro mindset: "this hand's result doesn't matter — what matters is whether my decision is +EV. If I keep making +EV decisions, I'll profit long-term." This mindset is what fundamentally separates pros from amateurs.
l5-session-review: Why Is Reviewing More Important Than Playing?
Many players spend lots of time playing but rarely review. Research shows that 1 hour of playing + 30 minutes of review progresses faster than 2 hours of pure playing.
Standard Session Review flow: 1) mark key hands → 2) analyze decision points → 3) compare with GTO → 4) record wins/losses → 5) make an improvement plan

Step 1: Mark key hands
• Right after each session, mark 3-5 "uncertain" hands
• Don't just look at big pots lost — also big pots won

Step 2: Analyze decision points
• At each street's key point ask "was there another option?"

Step 3: Compare with GTO
• Use this platform's GTO simulator to check the optimal play

Step 4: Record wins and losses
• Write down "what I did" and "what I should have done"

Step 5: Make an improvement plan
• List the most common errors as next session's focus
Don't be fooled by results during review ("I won, so I did it right"). Focus on decision quality, not results. A wrong decision can occasionally win money, but always loses long-term.

Session A/B/C tier analysis framework:
A tier (best state): focused, calm, every decision analyzed → suited to complex decisions
B tier (normal): some fatigue but basic decision quality maintained → suited to routine training
C tier (fatigued): attention dropping, intuition replacing analysis → stop immediately

Session management principles:
- No session over 60 minutes
- Rest 5 minutes every 30 minutes
- Force-end at C-tier signals
- Daily question caps: 0/50/100/200 four tiers

Theory reference: the Session A/B/C tier management method is in Theory Academy T8 “Session Management: Treating State as a Resource”, including session planning, stop-loss discipline, and a quantitative framework for long-term profitable mindset.

Counter-intuitive: winning sessions may be your worst learning opportunities. When you win consecutively, you get the illusion of "playing great", even when winning on luck. Real learning happens in losing sessions — that's when you find and fix errors.
l5-data-driven: Use Data to Find Your Leaks
Your own stats are the most objective mirror. By analyzing your VPIP, PFR, C-Bet %, per-position win rates, etc., you can precisely locate weaknesses.

VPIP/PFR gap too large (>8): calling too much, raising too little
C-Bet % < 50%: not aggressive enough postflop
Big per-position win-rate variance: strategy problems in certain positions
Showdown % > 35%: calling down to the river too often
Leak-fixing priority: fix the highest-frequency spots first (like preflop ranges), then lower-frequency spots. A preflop leak affects every hand; a river leak may rarely occur.
Do a monthly "data check-up": export your stats and compare with last month and target values. Progress is the process of leaks shrinking.
l5-tools:
Modern poker has entered the data age. Analysis tools help you:

1. Verify intuition: use math to check whether your play is correct
2. Find leaks: discover strategy leaks through data
3. Learn GTO: understand the theoretical optimal as a reference baseline
4. Track progress: record and analyze your long-term performance
Tools are great learning aids, but over-reliance hinders intuition. Correct usage: understand the principle first, then use the tool to verify.

PioSOLVER / GTO+:
- Purpose: solve the GTO strategy for a specific spot
- Use: postflop strategy analysis, frequency-balance research
- Learning tip: start with simple spots (e.g. heads-up flop), gradually add complexity

Equilab (free):
- Purpose: calculate a hand's equity vs a range
- Use: preflop range analysis, pot-odds calculation
- Learning tip: familiarize yourself with common range equities to build intuition

Hand2Note / Holdem Resource Manager:
- Purpose: track and analyze your historical data
- Use: find strategy leaks, monitor performance
- Learning tip: focus on key metrics (VPIP/PFR/3-bet%), don't over-analyze

The most effective learning path: use tools to analyze your problem hands, understand the correct play, then deliberately practice it live. Don't just look at results — understand the reasoning behind them.
Warning: don't open multiple tools at once while learning. Focused understanding of one spot beats skimming 100 spots.
l5-online-vs-live:
Online poker:
- Fast pace, about 10-15 seconds per hand
- About 60-80 hands per hour
- Needs fast decision-making
- Multi-tabling (MTT) boosts efficiency

Live poker:
- Slow pace, about 1-2 minutes per hand
- About 25-35 hands per hour
- More time to think
- Needs patience and mental toughness
Core difference: online profits from speed and volume; live profits from quality and patience. The two environments need different skills and mindsets.

Online multi-tabling tips:
- Start with 2-4 tables, gradually increase
- Choose tables at different positions (avoid acting simultaneously)
- Use quick decisions, reduce thinking time
- Note: multi-tabling lowers per-table focus — suited to standard hands

Live single-table tips:
- Focus on observing each opponent
- More time to read tells and images
- Suited to exploitative play

The HUD (Heads-Up Display) is an online-specific tool:

Using the HUD:
- Quickly identify opponent types (VPIP/PFR/3-bet%)
- Find opponent leaks (e.g. excessive fold-to-C-Bet)
- Make data-driven decisions

Counter-HUD strategy:
- Balance your data (don't let it get extreme)
- Exploit opponents who over-rely on HUD (e.g. frequent 3-bets vs players the HUD shows as tight)
- Vary your play regularly to make the data stale

Fast-fold poker features:
- New table every hand, extremely fast pace
- Can't adjust to specific opponents
- Suited to GTO play
- Needs fast decisions

Adaptation strategy:
- Simplify decision processes
- Rely on standard play
- Don't try to over-exploit in fast-fold
Live Tell Reading and Image Management

Live-specific skills:

Tell reading:
- Observe betting actions, expressions, posture
- Common tells: trembling hands (usually strong), hesitation (usually weak)
- Note: don't over-read — combine with data

Image management:
- Build a stable image (tight/loose/aggressive/passive)
- Exploit the image (e.g. bluff more with a tight image)
- Stay consistent so opponents can't read your patterns
The best players stay profitable both online and live. Try both environments to build a complete skill set.

l5-br-q4.question: What is the condition to move up?
options: Accumulate 30 buy-ins of the next stake in your current game
l5-br-q4.explanation: Move up when you've accumulated 30 buy-ins of the next stake, ensuring enough safety margin.

l5-br-q5.question: Why not mix living expenses with poker bankroll?
options: Keeping them separate is the first bankroll principle
l5-br-q5.explanation: Separate funds is the first principle of bankroll management. Mixing leads to irrational decisions under pressure.

l5-br-q6.question: Under the Kelly criterion, what is the optimal bankroll fraction f* at a 55% win rate with 1:1 net odds?

l5-br-q7.question: Under the Kelly criterion, what is the optimal bankroll fraction f* at a 40% win rate with 2:1 net odds?
l5-br-q7.explanation: f* = (bp − q) / b = (2×0.4 − 0.6) / 2 = 0.2 / 2 = 0.10, i.e. 10%. A win rate below 50% can still be worth betting because 2:1 odds compensate for it.

l5-br-q8.question: For a $20 buy-in tournament, how much bankroll does this lesson's minimum requirement (50 buy-ins) demand?
l5-br-q8.explanation: Tournament minimum 50 buy-ins = 50 × $20 = $1,000; this lesson recommends 50-100 buy-ins for tournaments.

l5-br-q9.question: What is the main purpose of the Half Kelly (f = f*/2) sizing recommended in this lesson?
options: Increase the profit of each bet
Further reduce the risk of ruin
l5-br-q9.explanation: Half Kelly stakes only half of the Kelly fraction (20% becomes 10% at a 60% win rate with 1:1 odds), trading some growth for lower variance and a lower risk of ruin.

l5-br-q10.question: Playing $2/$5 cash (100BB buy-in = $500), how much bankroll do 30 buy-ins require?
l5-br-q10.explanation: 30 buy-ins × $500 = $15,000. This lesson recommends 30-50 buy-ins for cash games, and 50+ buy-ins as the professional standard.

l5-tilt-q1.question: After a bad beat, what is the best move?
options: Play more hands to win back
l5-tilt-q1.explanation: The best move is to pause and check your emotional state. If angry or frustrated, stop the session.

l5-tilt-q2.question: What is a "stop-loss line"?
options: The maximum loss you've set for a session
l5-tilt-q2.explanation: A stop-loss is the maximum session loss you preset (e.g. 2 buy-ins). Stop when reached to prevent bigger tilt losses.

l5-tilt-q3.question: Which is NOT a tilt type?
l5-tilt-q3.explanation: Tilt types include anger, fear, revenge, and desperation — not "happy".

l5-tilt-q4.question: When you catch yourself doing "out-of-character" actions, you should?
l5-tilt-q4.explanation: Out-of-character actions are a tilt stop signal — stop immediately.

l5-tilt-q5.question: How often should you take a 5-10 minute break?
l5-tilt-q5.explanation: Take a 5-10 minute break every hour to keep a clear head and stable emotions.

l5-tilt-q6.question: According to the warning signs in this lesson, an accuracy drop beyond which threshold means you should pause training?
l5-tilt-q6.explanation: This lesson lists two stop signals: three wrong answers in a row and an accuracy drop of more than 15%. At that point decision quality is already falling and continuing only enlarges the loss.

l5-tilt-q7.question: In Tendler's seven tilt profiles, which one is "overconfidence after a winning streak"?
l5-tilt-q7.explanation: Entitlement tilt comes from overconfidence after winning; fear tilt comes from being afraid to lose, boredom tilt from attention decay in long sessions, and self-destructive tilt from subconsciously punishing yourself.

l5-tilt-q8.question: Which Tendler tilt profile matches "negative emotion accumulated over a long downswing"?
l5-tilt-q8.explanation: Frustration tilt is negative emotion accumulated over a long downswing; anger tilt is triggered by a single bad beat, urgency tilt by time or money pressure, and revenge tilt targets one specific opponent.

l5-tilt-q9.question: Which Tendler tilt profile matches "attention decay caused by a long session"?
l5-tilt-q9.explanation: Boredom tilt comes from attention decay during long sessions, the same risk as "keep playing while tired" in this lesson; timed breaks and a stop-loss line control it.

l5-tilt-q10.question: To win back your losses before the end of the month you open four more tables and cut the thinking time for every decision. Which tilt profile does this most resemble?
l5-tilt-q10.explanation: Urgency tilt is rushed decision-making driven by time or money pressure; adding tables and compressing thinking time is its classic form. The fix is to drop back to one table and end the session at your stop-loss line.

l5-game-q1.question: One trait of a good table is?
l5-game-q1.explanation: Ideal tables have many recreational players (high VPIP), maximizing your skill edge.

l5-game-q2.question: How many hands of sample do you need to accurately assess your level?
l5-game-q2.explanation: At least 10,000+ hands. Short-term results are too variance-affected to assess skill.

l5-game-q3.question: What is the ideal ranking for you at the table?
l5-game-q3.explanation: Ideally you're the best player at the table, maximizing your skill edge.

l5-game-q4.question: What does a short-term (1 week) win/loss show?
l5-game-q4.explanation: Short-term results are too variance-affected — need 10,000+ hands to assess.

l5-game-q5.question: What matters more than results?
l5-game-q5.explanation: Focus on decision quality, not results. Wrong decisions may occasionally win but always lose long-term.

l5-game-q6.question: What VPIP threshold does this lesson use to call a table "full of recreational players"?
l5-game-q6.explanation: This lesson's standard: a good table has a high share of recreational players, i.e. VPIP > 30%. They enter too many pots, which is exactly where your edge shows up.

l5-game-q7.question: Why is a high flop rate (many players seeing the flop) a sign of a good table?
options: It means the opponents are tight
It means many players enter with weak hands, so your edge is easier to realize
It means the rake is lower
It means the blinds are larger
l5-game-q7.explanation: Many players seeing flops means opponents play wide ranges — the hallmark of weak players. Those pots contain more mistakes, so your technical edge converts into profit more easily.

l5-game-q8.question: You sit down and find that the whole table consists of long-term winning professionals. What is the most reasonable move?
options: Stay and outplay them to prove yourself
Move to a table with recreational players
Move up in stakes to regain your edge
Shove every hand to create variance
l5-game-q8.explanation: Game selection comes before technical play: a full table of professionals erases your edge, so switching to a weaker table is the +EV choice. Grinding it out just burns time and confidence.

l5-game-q9.question: You lost 5 buy-ins this week, but your review shows every decision was correct. Per this lesson, what should you do?
options: Move up in stakes to win it back
Switch to a different style until you are even
l5-game-q9.explanation: 5 buy-ins (500BB) sits inside normal variance, and you need 10,000+ hands to judge your level. If the decisions are right, keep executing; changing strategy because of short-term results turns into long-term -EV.

l5-game-q10.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a good table?
options: Players raising often and interacting a lot
A full table of tight-aggressive professionals
l5-game-q10.explanation: The four features of a good table are many recreational players (VPIP > 30%), large average pots, a high flop rate and lots of interaction; a full table of tight-aggressive professionals is exactly what you want to avoid.

l5-sr-q1.question: What is the first step of Session Review?
l5-sr-q1.explanation: Review starts by marking the key hands to analyze, then deep analysis.

l5-sr-q2.question: What should review focus on?
l5-sr-q2.explanation: Quality review focuses on whether the decision process was correct, not the single result.

l5-sr-q3.question: Per the Session A/B/C framework, what should you do when C-tier (fatigue) signals appear?
options: Play on until the planned number of hands is done
Raise stakes to win back what you lost
Add more tables to spread your attention
l5-sr-q3.explanation: This lesson's Session A/B/C framework defines C tier as dropping attention with intuition replacing analysis — force-stop the session as soon as the signals show. Playing on or raising stakes only compounds losses under degraded decisions; adding tables further dilutes attention; and a pre-set hand quota cannot override what your current state is telling you.

l5-sr-q4.question: How many key hands should you mark per session?

l5-sr-q5.question: What is the 5th step of review?
l5-sr-q5.explanation: The 5th step is making an improvement plan.

l5-sr-q6.question: Per this lesson's session management rules, how long should a single session last at most?
l5-sr-q6.explanation: This lesson's rules: no more than 60 minutes per session, a 5-minute break every 30 minutes, and an immediate stop at any C-grade signal.

l5-sr-q7.question: Per the session management rules, how long should you rest after every 30 minutes of play?
l5-sr-q7.explanation: This lesson prescribes a 5-minute break every 30 minutes, using short breaks to stay in the top two grades instead of sliding into C grade (attention decay, deciding on instinct).

l5-sr-q8.question: In the A/B/C session framework, what characterizes A grade?
options: Some fatigue but basic decision quality is maintained
Emotional swings and the urge to get even
l5-sr-q8.explanation: A grade is the best state: focused, calm and analytical, suited to complex decisions; B grade maintains basic quality for routine play; C grade means stop immediately.

l5-sr-q9.question: In the five-step review method, what is step 3?
l5-sr-q9.explanation: The five steps are: tag the key hands → analyze the decision points → compare against GTO → record what was learned → build an improvement plan. Step 3 checks the optimal line with a solver.

l5-sr-q10.question: Why does this lesson call a winning session "possibly the worst learning opportunity"?
options: Hand quality is higher when winning, so there is nothing to analyze
Winning hides bad decisions and makes you believe you played well
You are too excited after winning to review
Hand data from winning sessions cannot be imported into tools
l5-sr-q10.explanation: Winning creates the illusion that you played well even when you were simply lucky; real learning happens in losing sessions, where mistakes surface and can be corrected.

l5-dd-q1.question: A big VPIP/PFR gap indicates?
options: Calling too much, raising too little
l5-dd-q1.explanation: VPIP far above PFR means too much passive calling — raise or fold instead.

l5-dd-q2.question: Which leak type should you prioritize fixing?
l5-dd-q2.explanation: Preflop decisions happen every hand — fixing preflop leaks has the biggest return.

l5-dd-q3.question: C-Bet % < 50% indicates?
l5-dd-q3.explanation: C-Bet below 50% means not aggressive enough postflop.

l5-dd-q4.question: Showdown % > 35% indicates?
options: Calling down to the river too often
l5-dd-q4.explanation: A too-high showdown % means calling down to the river too often.

l5-dd-q5.question: What should you do monthly to track progress?
l5-dd-q5.explanation: Do a monthly data check-up — export stats and compare with targets.

l5-dd-q6.question: By how many percentage points must VPIP and PFR differ before this lesson calls it "too much passive calling"?
l5-dd-q6.explanation: This lesson's standard: a VPIP/PFR gap above 8 percentage points means too much calling and too little raising — more of those hands should be raised or folded preflop.

l5-dd-q7.question: Your win rate varies noticeably by position. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: It is pure luck and can be ignored
The sample is large enough to move up
l5-dd-q7.explanation: Overall win rate hides positional differences; a wide spread by position usually points to leaks in the open-raise and defense strategy of certain seats, most often the blinds.

l5-dd-q8.question: How often does this lesson recommend a data checkup?
l5-dd-q8.explanation: Export your stats monthly and compare them with last month and with the targets. Progress is the steady shrinking of leaks, and only a fixed rhythm makes the trend visible.

l5-dd-q9.question: Your VPIP is 45% and your PFR is 25%. Per this lesson's standard, what does this show?
options: A 20-point gap (>8): too much passive calling
A 20-point gap that sits in the healthy range
VPIP is too low, so you play too tight
The data is completely normal, no change needed
l5-dd-q9.explanation: 45 − 25 = 20 points, far above this lesson's 8-point threshold: a large share of the hands you enter are passive calls, and some of them should become raises or folds.

l5-dd-q10.question: From a data perspective, what is the most accurate definition of progress?
options: Leaks being found and closed one after another
l5-dd-q10.explanation: Short-term winnings are dominated by variance; progress as measured by data is the continuous discovery and repair of leaks, which is exactly what the monthly checkup is for.

l5-tools-q1.question: What is the main use of PioSOLVER / GTO+?
options: Solve the GTO strategy for specific spots
l5-tools-q1.explanation: PioSOLVER/GTO+ are solvers for analyzing GTO strategies in specific spots.

l5-tools-q2.question: What is Equilab's main function?

l5-tools-q3.question: What is the correct way to use analysis tools?

Only look at results without understanding

l5-tools-q4.question: What is the main use of Hand2Note / Holdem Resource Manager?

l5-tools-q5.question: Which tool-use suggestion is WRONG?
options: Focused understanding of one spot beats skimming 100
Open multiple tools at once for efficiency
l5-tools-q5.explanation: Opening multiple tools at once lowers learning efficiency. Focus on one spot and analyze deeply.

l5-tools-q6.question: What does this lesson recommend for learning PioSOLVER / GTO+?
options: Start with simple scenarios such as heads-up flops and add complexity gradually
Memorize the frequencies of every range first
l5-tools-q6.explanation: The learning path for solvers moves from simple scenarios (e.g. a heads-up flop) to more complexity; starting with hard multiway spots only produces output you cannot interpret.

l5-tools-q7.question: When using a tracker such as Hand2Note, what does this lesson advise?
options: Focus on the key stats (VPIP/PFR/3-bet%) and avoid over-analysis
Only look at winnings and losses
Only open the tool after losing
l5-tools-q7.explanation: This lesson advises focusing on key stats (VPIP/PFR/3-bet%) and avoiding over-analysis: too many metrics dilute your attention and hide the leaks that actually matter.

l5-tools-q8.question: What is the point of repeatedly running equity calculations on common ranges in Equilab?
options: To internalize the equities of common ranges and build intuition
l5-tools-q8.explanation: Equilab is used for preflop range and equity work; repeating those numbers turns equity into intuition so you can judge strength in game without a lookup table.

l5-tools-q9.question: After analyzing a hand, what happens if you only take the "correct action" without understanding the logic?
options: Learning efficiency drops and the lesson fails to transfer to other spots
Nothing, as long as the conclusion matches
You move up in stakes faster
l5-tools-q9.explanation: The mistake shown in this lesson's example is exactly "only looking at results, not the process": memorizing the conclusion without the reason does not transfer once the parameters change, so learning efficiency drops.

l5-tools-q10.question: How does this lesson position analysis tools overall?
options: Tools can replace understanding the theory
Tools are powerful learning aids, but over-reliance blocks intuition
The more tools you run, the faster you learn
l5-tools-q10.explanation: Tools help you verify intuition, find leaks, learn GTO and track progress; over-reliance blocks intuition, so the right approach is to understand the theory first and then verify it with tools.

l5-online-vs-live-q1.question: How many hands per hour does online poker have?
l5-online-vs-live-q1.explanation: Online is fast — about 60-80 hands per hour.

l5-online-vs-live-q2.question: What is the main use of a HUD?
options: Quickly identify opponent types and data
l5-online-vs-live-q2.explanation: A HUD shows opponent VPIP/PFR/3-bet% etc. to identify opponent types.

l5-online-vs-live-q3.question: What strategy suits fast-fold poker (Zoom/Blitz)?
l5-online-vs-live-q3.explanation: Fast-fold changes tables every hand, so you can't target specific opponents — play GTO.

l5-online-vs-live-q4.question: What is the advantage of live poker?
l5-online-vs-live-q4.explanation: Live is slow-paced with more time to observe opponent tells and build images.

l5-online-vs-live-q5.question: What is the core of counter-HUD strategy?
options: Balance your data so opponents can't exploit you
l5-online-vs-live-q5.explanation: Counter-HUD means balancing your data so it doesn't get extreme and can't be exploited.

l5-online-vs-live-q6.question: Roughly how many hands per hour do you play live?
l5-online-vs-live-q6.explanation: Live poker takes about 1-2 minutes per hand, i.e. roughly 25-35 hands per hour; online takes about 10-15 seconds per hand, i.e. roughly 60-80 hands per hour.

l5-online-vs-live-q7.question: How does this lesson summarize the difference in profit sources between online and live?
options: Online relies on quality and patience, live on speed and volume
Online relies on speed and volume, live on quality and patience
Both rely only on luck of the deal
Both rely only on reading tells
l5-online-vs-live-q7.explanation: Online is fast and supports multi-tabling, so profit comes from volume and speed; live is slow, so profit comes from decision quality, tell reading and patience. The skills and mindset differ accordingly.

l5-online-vs-live-q8.question: How many tables does this lesson suggest starting with when multi-tabling online?
l5-online-vs-live-q8.explanation: Start with 2-4 tables and add gradually; multi-tabling lowers focus per table, suits standard spots and is the wrong environment for complex decisions.

l5-online-vs-live-q9.question: According to the live tell examples in this lesson, shaking hands while betting usually means?
options: A fake-out to induce a call
l5-online-vs-live-q9.explanation: The common tells listed in this lesson: shaking hands usually lean strong, hesitation usually leans weak; do not over-read them, and combine them with data and the opponent's image.

l5-online-vs-live-q10.question: What is the most important rule of live image management?
options: Keep changing styles so opponents can never read you
Stay consistent and never let opponents read a fixed pattern
l5-online-vs-live-q10.explanation: Image management builds a stable image and exploits it (e.g. bluff more when perceived as tight); consistency is the premise — contradictory behavior leaks information by itself.

reasoning: You play NL50 (buy-in $50), bankroll dropped from $2000 to $900

l5-bankroll-ex2.mistakeReasoning: Refusing to move down is a classic ego problem. Many world-class players moved down and climbed back. Protecting the bankroll always comes first.

Correct move: deep breath, leave the table 5 minutes, assess emotions

l5-tilt-ex2.mistakeReasoning: "One more hand" is the most dangerous self-deception when tilting. Once past the stop-loss, your decision quality plummets.

l5-game-ex2.mistakeReasoning: A short-term downswing doesn't mean the strategy is wrong. Variance is part of poker — only a large enough sample proves whether a strategy is +EV.

d-l5-tilt-q1.scenario: You just lost a big pot to a bad beat
d-l5-tilt-q1.question: What should you do next?
option: Deal the next hand right away
Take a 5-10 minute break and reset your emotions
Move up stakes to win it back
d-l5-tilt-q1.explanation: Tilt is likely after a bad beat. Take a few minutes to let the emotion settle so you are not making decisions in an emotional state.

d-l5-tilt-q2.scenario: You notice you have called large bets with weak hands three times in a row
d-l5-tilt-q2.question: What kind of signal is this?
option: Normal variance
A tilt warning - you need to stop
A strategy adjustment
d-l5-tilt-q2.explanation: Calling big bets with weak hands repeatedly is a classic tilt behaviour. Stop immediately and check your emotional state.

d-l5-tilt-q3.scenario: You just lost a big pot and now want revenge
d-l5-tilt-q3.question: What does that thought belong to?
option: A normal competitive mindset
A typical sign of tilt
A strategy adjustment
d-l5-tilt-q3.explanation: A revenge mindset is a typical sign of tilt. It makes you decide for the wrong reasons instead of based on EV.

d-l5-tilt-q4.scenario: You notice your heart racing and your breathing getting faster
d-l5-tilt-q4.question: These are the physiological signals of what?
option: Focus
Emotional agitation / a tilt warning
Fatigue
d-l5-tilt-q4.explanation: A racing heart and faster breathing are physiological signals of emotional agitation. This is a tilt warning - stop and take deep breaths.

d-l5-tilt-q5.scenario: You have lost three sessions in a row
d-l5-tilt-q5.question: What should you do?
option: Keep playing, you will win it back eventually
Stop playing and take a day off
Move up stakes to recover the losses
d-l5-tilt-q5.explanation: Playing on after losing sessions in a row easily triggers tilt. Take a day off to let the emotions settle instead of deciding in an emotional state.

d-l5-tilt-q6.scenario: You catch yourself cursing at opponents or complaining out loud
d-l5-tilt-q6.question: What signal is this?
option: Normal emotional release
A sign of tilt - you need to stop
A sign of focus
d-l5-tilt-q6.explanation: Cursing at opponents or venting is a sign of tilt. It shows your emotions are already affecting your decisions, so stop immediately.

d-l5-tilt-q7.scenario: An opponent has successfully bluffed you three times in a row
d-l5-tilt-q7.question: What should you do next?
option: Call him wider next time
Check your own emotions and take a break if needed
Fight back immediately and re-raise him next time
d-l5-tilt-q7.explanation: Being bluffed repeatedly easily triggers tilt. Check your emotional state first, and take a break if you are angry. Never decide out of emotion.

d-l5-tilt-q8.scenario: You notice you are playing looser than usual
d-l5-tilt-q8.question: What is the reason?
option: A strategy adjustment
It is probably caused by tilt
Bad luck
d-l5-tilt-q8.explanation: Playing looser than usual is a classic sign of tilt. Emotion makes you relax your starting-hand standards and enter pots with weak hands.

d-l5-session-q1.scenario: You have lost three big pots in a row and your emotions are starting to swing
d-l5-session-q1.question: What should you do now?
option: Keep playing, luck will turn around
Execute your stop-loss immediately and end the session
Move up stakes to win the money back
d-l5-session-q1.explanation: Emotional swings after losing big pots in a row are a tilt warning. The stop-loss is the key discipline that protects both your bankroll and your mental game. End the session right away and play another day.

d-l5-session-q2.scenario: You sit down at a table and find it is full of TAG players
d-l5-session-q2.question: Facing a table full of TAGs, how should you choose?
option: Stay and play to prove yourself
Change tables and look for one with a calling station
Move up stakes
d-l5-session-q2.explanation: A table full of TAGs leaves an almost negligible edge. The core of game selection is finding tables with more weak players, so changing tables is a +EV decision.

d-l5-session-q3.scenario: You planned a 4-hour session; after 3 hours you feel tired
d-l5-session-q3.question: What should you do once you feel fatigued?
option: Push through the planned time
End the session now or at least take a 15-minute break
Drink an energy drink and keep playing
d-l5-session-q3.explanation: Fatigue drags down attention and decision quality, so playing on while tired is -EV. End the session or rest until you have recovered.

d-l5-session-q4.scenario: Your bankroll is $2000 and you currently play NL100 ($100 buy-in)
d-l5-session-q4.question: Is your bankroll management sound?
option: Yes, 20 buy-ins is enough
No, drop to NL50 or lower and keep at least 30-50 buy-ins
You should move up to NL200
d-l5-session-q4.explanation: $2000 at NL100 is only 20 buy-ins, below the standard 30-50 buy-in requirement. Drop to NL50 (40 buy-ins) to withstand variance.

d-l5-session-q5.scenario: You won a big session (+10 buy-ins) and feel pumped up
d-l5-session-q5.question: What should you do after winning a big session?
option: Ride the hot streak into another session
Finish playing, take notes and keep your normal routine
Move up stakes - winners should take risks
d-l5-session-q5.explanation: A big win easily breeds overconfidence (the positive version of the gambler's fallacy). The right move is to wrap up, record the lessons and rest normally. Do not change your plan just because you won.

d-l5-session-q6.scenario: Two online tables are available: table A averages a $15 pot, table B averages $8
d-l5-session-q6.question: You are a winning NL25 player - which table should you pick?
option: Table A (bigger pots), it must be more profitable
Observe both tables first and choose the one with more weak players
Just pick either one
d-l5-session-q6.explanation: A bigger average pot does not automatically mean more profit. What matters is player type - tables with more weak players are the profitable ones. Observe before you sit.

d-l5-session-q7.scenario: You set your session stop-loss at 3 buy-ins
d-l5-session-q7.question: Why do you need a stop-loss line?
option: It stops you losing more when you are off your game
It limits how fast you win
It has no practical meaning
d-l5-session-q7.explanation: The stop-loss is core bankroll-management discipline. It keeps a bad session (tilt or fatigue) from costing you more than you planned to risk.

d-l5-session-q8.scenario: You just finished a session for -5 buy-ins and a friend invites you to a home game
d-l5-session-q8.question: Should you go play the home game right after losing a big session?
option: Yes, a home game is an easy way to win it back
No - rest and review the session instead
Yes, but at higher stakes
d-l5-session-q8.explanation: Do not jump straight back into play after losing a big session. Rest, review and reset your mindset. Carrying negative emotion into a home game easily leads to tilt.

d-l5-session-q9.scenario: You play 20 hours of poker a week and lately your win rate has dropped
d-l5-session-q9.question: What might explain the falling win rate, and how should you adjust?
option: Bad luck - no adjustment needed
Probably over-play / fatigue - cut play hours and add study and rest
Move up stakes to make up the losses
d-l5-session-q9.explanation: A falling win rate usually points to fatigue or lower-quality play. Cutting hours and adding study and rest is the right adjustment; do not try to make it up at higher stakes.

Spot dangerous bankroll habits (mixing living money, borrowing to play, refusing to move down) and give replacements such as a fully separate poker bankroll
Compute the optimal bankroll fraction with the Kelly formula f* = (bp − q) / b (60% edge at even money gives 20%) and explain why Half Kelly is more conservative
l5-tilt: Identify the four tilt types (anger, fear, revenge, desperation) and the triggers of the Tendler 7-type tilt profiles
Give the five anti-tilt tactics (a stop-loss line, scheduled breaks, self-awareness, long-term view, stop signals) and judge your own current emotional state
Judge that a win-rate drop beyond 15% or a run of out-of-character actions means stopping the session now, not grinding on
l5-game-selection: Identify the four marks of a good table (recreational players above 30% VPIP, large average pots, high flop rate, lots of action) and compare being the best versus the sixth-best player at the table
Judge that at least 10,000+ hands are needed to assess skill, and explain that short-term results are variance-dominated
Explain that sustained +EV decisions matter more than any single outcome, and judge against changing a correct strategy after a short downswing
l5-session-review: Order the five-step review flow (mark key hands, analyze decision points, compare with GTO, record takeaways, plan improvements) and state what each step involves
Judge that reviews should grade decision quality over results, and explain why winning sessions can hide mistakes while losing sessions teach the most
Use the Session A/B/C framework to judge your state (C-grade fatigue signals force a stop) and state the 60-minute per-session cap
l5-data-driven: State the abnormal bands of key stats (a VPIP-PFR gap over 8 means too many passive calls, C-bet under 50% means not aggressive enough postflop, showdown above 35% means calling down too light)
Judge the repair priority: fix the highest-frequency spots first (preflop happens every hand) before low-frequency spots
Judge that win-rate gaps by position point to weak-position strategy problems, and state the monthly data check-up to track progress
drill-l5-tilt: Identify pre-tilt scenarios (a bad beat, calling big bets with weak hands, wanting revenge, a losing streak) and give the right response of resting or stopping
Tell tilt responses from dangerous ones (moving up to win it back or starting the next hand immediately are both hazardous)
l5-tools: Tell the three tool classes apart (PioSOLVER/GTO+ for solving GTO strategies, Equilab for range equity, Hand2Note/HRM for tracking and analyzing history)

l5-online-vs-live: Compare online and live pacing (about 60-80 hands per hour versus 25-35) and their profit logics (speed and volume online, quality and patience live)
Judge what a HUD is for (rapidly reading opponent types and leaks) and the core of anti-HUD play (balancing your own stats so they cannot be used against you)
Judge that fast-fold poker suits GTO strategies (no specific opponent to exploit) while live play can exploit through tell reading and image management
drill-l5-session: Judge the right session-management decisions (stop-loss after losing big pots in a row, table-changing from a full TAG lineup, ending or resting when fatigued)
Compute the bankroll-to-stake match ($2,000 at NL100 is only 20 buy-ins, so drop to NL50 or lower to hold 30-50 buy-ins)
Spot the right behavior after big wins and big losses (take notes and rest as normal, refuse to jump straight back in)
